faq.a: It blocks RNA polymerase II, halting mRNA synthesis, leading to loss of essential proteins and hepatocyte death.
faq.q: Why does amanitin cause liver failure?

faq.a: Stopping the drug and providing supportive care (hydration, monitoring liver enzymes) is the main approach; there is no specific antidote.
Early onset of severe nausea, vomiting, and a rapid rise in jaundice without an obvious infectious cause.
faq.q: What bedside sign suggests a transcription toxin exposure?

exam: A farmer presents with sudden jaundice after eating wild mushrooms — what is the most likely toxin and its mechanism? — Amanitin; blocks RNA polymerase II, stopping mRNA synthesis.
Why is rifampicin contraindicated in patients with severe liver disease? — It is hepatotoxic and can worsen hepatic failure caused by transcription inhibition.

How would you differentiate amanitin poisoning from viral hepatitis in a low‑resource setting? — History of mushroom ingestion, rapid onset of GI symptoms, and lack of fever; viral hepatitis often has prodromal fever and slower progression.
A patient on TB therapy develops orange urine and a false‑negative dipstick for protein — what explains this? — Rifampicin induces urine colour change and interferes with dipstick chemistry.

What immediate management steps are required for suspected amanitin poisoning when labs are unavailable? — Decontaminate GI tract (activated charcoal if early), aggressive IV fluids, monitor mental status, and arrange transfer for possible liver support.

Explain why transcription inhibitors are useful in cancer therapy but pose a risk of bone‑marrow suppression. — They halt rapidly dividing cells’ protein synthesis, targeting tumors; the same effect harms hematopoietic precursors.

A child with sickle cell disease receives an herbal remedy and develops acute liver failure — what should you consider? — Possible transcription‑blocking toxin in the herb (e.g., amanitin‑containing mushroom); obtain exposure history and manage as toxin‑induced hepatitis.

Why might a patient on high‑dose rifampicin have a falsely low serum creatinine? — Rifampicin induces hepatic enzymes that increase creatinine clearance; rely on clinical assessment if labs are unreliable.
ai.title: Inhibitors of Transcription
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Transcription inhibitors block the synthesis of RNA from DNA, affecting cell growth and viral replication. Understanding their mechanisms helps diagnose drug toxicity and select therapies in resource‑limited settings.

b: Key concept: blocking transcription stops protein production.
Clinically relevant in infections (e.g., bacterial toxins) and cancer chemotherapy.
sections.p: Transcription is the first step of gene expression where RNA polymerase copies DNA into messenger RNA. Inhibitors can be endogenous, microbial toxins, or drugs, and they may cause disease or be used therapeutically.

b: Alpha‑amanitin binds RNA polymerase II → halts mRNA synthesis.
Rifampicin binds bacterial RNA polymerase β‑subunit → blocks bacterial transcription.
sections.p: Inhibitors act at distinct stages: initiation (preventing polymerase binding), elongation (stalling the enzyme), or termination (premature release of RNA). They may bind DNA, the polymerase active site, or required cofactors.

b: Tumor suppressor loss may increase sensitivity to transcription blockers.
Viral proteins (e.g., HIV Tat) can be targeted by specific inhibitors.
sections.p: Cells regulate transcription via transcription factors, epigenetic marks, and feedback loops. Inhibitors can disrupt these controls, leading to cell death or disease.

b: Amanita phalloides poisoning → severe hepatic necrosis.
sections.p: Excessive inhibition causes cytotoxicity, hepatic failure, or bone marrow suppression. Infections may produce toxins that act as transcription inhibitors, leading to organ damage.

b: Ask about wild mushroom consumption, herbal teas, and recent antibiotics.
Look for early signs: nausea, vomiting, jaundice, dark urine.
sections.p: Recognising transcription inhibition is vital when patients present with unexplained liver injury, cytopenias, or after exposure to known toxins/drugs. In low‑resource settings, history of mushroom ingestion or use of traditional herbal remedies is common.

t.b: Detect hepatocellular injury from transcription toxin; if unavailable, use bedside assessment of jaundice and urine colour.
Identify bone‑marrow suppression; if unavailable, monitor for bruising, infections, and fatigue.
Assess hepatic encephalopathy risk; if unavailable, watch for altered mental status.

b: Distinguish amanitin poisoning (RNA Pol II) from acetaminophen toxicity (glutathione depletion).
Explain why rifampicin is useful in TB but can cause false‑negative urine dipsticks.
sections.p: Examiners may test your ability to link a toxin or drug to its transcription‑blocking action, differentiate it from other mechanisms, and outline immediate management steps.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening jaundice, hepatic encephalopathy, or coagulopathy
Severe pancytopenia with bleeding or infection
